Common questions

    
What is a creator media kit?

    
A one-page summary a content creator sends to a brand considering a sponsorship — bio, platform reach and engagement, audience demographics, past partnerships, and a rate card — so a brand can evaluate the fit and know what to offer without a back-and-forth email. More background: what belongs in a media kit, and what doesn't.

    
Is this free, and do I need an account?

    
Yes, and no. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is stored anywhere but your own browser. Fill in the form and download the result — there is no account, no watermark, and no upsell.

    
Where does my photo come from?

    
You paste a link to a photo you already host somewhere (your own site, an Instagram post, a public Google Drive/Dropbox link, an image host). This tool does not accept file uploads, so nothing you have not already made public ever leaves your device.

    
Should I include a rate card if I've never charged for a post before?

    
Yes, even a first guess. A brand reading a media kit with no rates still has to ask what you charge, which is exactly the back-and-forth this tool exists to skip — and a stated starting rate is easy to revise upward once you have a few paid partnerships to compare against.

    
How is this different from Kitly?

    
Kitly links your social accounts for a media kit that updates itself automatically; this tool needs no account and no social-media linking at all — you fill in a form and download a self-contained file right now. See this generator vs. Kitly for the full comparison.

    
Why not just build one in a document editor?

    
You can — a word processor or slide deck holds the same content. What it won't do on its own is warn you a rate card or contact email is missing, or keep a plain-text copy in sync with the formatted one. See this generator vs. assembling one by hand for the full comparison.

Media Kit Generator vs. assembling one by hand in a document editor

A word processor or slide deck can hold the same bio, platform stats, audience notes, past brand deals, and rate card this generator does — most media kits ever sent were built exactly that way. What it does not do on its own: flag a missing partnerships contact or rate card, keep a plain-text copy in sync with the formatted one every time you edit it, or lay out the page. This tool does all three the moment the form is filled in.

What each approach actually does

A document editor — a word processor, a slide deck, a blank page in any general-purpose tool — will hold anything you type: bio, platform reach, audience breakdown, past collaborations, testimonials, a rate card. Nothing about the blank page tells you what a brand expects to find, so a kit missing a way to actually contact you, or with no stated rate, ships exactly as easily as a complete one. Producing a plain-text version for an intake form that rejects attachments means building a second copy and manually keeping it matching every time the formatted one changes. Layout — type sizes, spacing, where the stats table sits relative to the bio — is a design decision you make yourself, each time you revise it.

This generator takes the same content through one form and builds both files at once: a self-contained, print-friendly HTML one-sheet and a plain-text edition, generated from the identical data so the two can never drift apart. Before it builds anything it requires a creator or channel name and a bio; separately, without blocking generation, it warns when there is no partnerships contact email, no platforms listed, no rate card, or no photo link — the specific gaps a brand notices first when deciding whether to pay you, not a spelling or grammar check. The form autosaves to your own browser as you type, so closing the tab mid-edit does not lose the draft.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I forgot to include a way to actually contact me.This generator — warns before you send the kit out, not after a brand gives up.
I never wrote down what I'd actually charge.This generator — warns when the rate card is empty, because a brand still won't know what to offer without one.
A brand's intake form won't take an attachment; I need plain text.This generator — built from the same data, every time, so it never falls out of sync.
I want full control over layout, typography, and a custom design.A document editor or design tool — this generator uses one fixed template, deliberately.
I closed the tab halfway through filling in the form.This generator — the draft autosaves locally and reloads where you left off.
What actually belongs in a media kit in the first place?This generator's own explanation of what a media kit is and isn't.

The two are not mutually exclusive: a document editor is still the right tool for a kit built around custom design work a fixed template cannot express. For the common case — a complete, correctly-formatted one-pager and a plain-text edition to send tonight, with the obvious gaps flagged before a brand finds them — filling in a form is faster than laying out a page.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the generator runs in your browser, and it keeps working with the connection off once loaded.

Common questions

Can I just build a sponsorship media kit in a word processor or slide deck myself?

Yes — a document editor holds the same bio, platform stats, audience notes, past brand deals, and rate card this generator does, and plenty of media kits in circulation were built exactly that way. What it does not do on its own is tell you the kit is missing something a brand expects, produce a plain-text copy alongside the formatted one, or lay out the page — all three are on you, every time you update it.

What does the generator check that a blank document does not?

A blank document accepts whatever you type and stays silent about what you left out. This generator requires a creator name and a bio before it will build anything, and separately warns — without blocking — when there is no partnerships contact email, no platforms listed, no rate card, or no photo link, because those are the specific gaps a brand notices first when deciding whether to pay you.

Why does a plain-text version matter?

Plenty of brand intake forms and partnership emails reject an attached file or strip its formatting, and a document built in a word processor or slide tool has no plain-text edition unless you build one separately and then keep it matching every time you update the original. This generator produces both from the same form in the same pass, so the two never drift apart.

Is a document editor ever the better choice?

Yes, for a layout this generator does not offer — a designed multi-page deck with custom typography and photo placement, or a kit built around a visual identity a document or design tool can express and this one, deliberately kept to one plain template, cannot. This generator trades that design flexibility for a page that appears the moment the form is filled in, with no layout decisions to make.

what-is-a-media-kit.html.text:
← Back to the media kit generator

What is a creator media kit, and what belongs in it?

A media kit is a one-page summary a content creator sends to a brand considering a sponsorship — the person deciding whether to book, cover, or playlist them, in the same role a venue booker or blog editor plays for a musician. It exists because that person is usually comparing several creators at once and deciding fast: who is this, what's their reach and audience, have they done this before, and what do they charge.

What belongs in it

  • A short bio — a few sentences to two short paragraphs. Lead with your niche and any concrete, checkable facts (years active, notable features, audience size) before adjectives.
  • One good photo — a clear headshot or on-brand content photo. It does not need a professional shoot to start.
  • Platform reach and engagement — follower count and engagement rate per platform. This is the section a brand's team reads first, and it is why a media kit exists at all.
  • Audience demographics, if you have them — age range, gender split, top location. Platform analytics show all three; brands use them to check fit against their own customer.
  • Past brand partnerships, if any — proves you've done sponsored work before and gives a brand a campaign to look at.
  • A rate card — even a first guess. Skipping it does not avoid the pricing conversation; it just delays it by one more email.

What doesn't belong in it

Your entire content history, a mission statement, or anything a reader has to scroll far to get past. A media kit is a fast decision aid, not a portfolio site — if you want the deeper version, link to your actual channel or site from it, not the other way around.

How it differs from a link-in-bio page

A link-in-bio page is built for a fan clicking through to your latest content and can be as shallow as you like. A media kit is built for one specific reader making one specific business decision, so it leads with exactly what that decision needs: reach, audience fit, proof, and a price.

Frequently asked questions

Who actually reads a media kit?

A brand's marketing or influencer-partnerships team, or an agency screening creators on a brand's behalf — almost always comparing several creators at once, so a scannable one-pager with numbers up front is the point, not a limitation.

How is a media kit different from a link-in-bio page?

A link-in-bio page is built for a fan clicking through to your content; a media kit is built for a brand deciding whether to pay you, so it leads with what that decision needs: reach, engagement, audience fit, and a rate — none of which a link-in-bio page is built to show.

Do I need a large following before making one?

No. A smaller, clearly-stated audience with a real niche and a genuine engagement rate is a normal, complete first media kit — many brands specifically seek out smaller creators for exactly that reason. The generator simply omits any section you leave blank rather than showing a placeholder.

Build one now →

No warranty. This page is informational, describing common practice among content creators and the brands that sponsor them — not a rule any brand or agency is bound by. Confirm what a specific brand's intake process actually wants before sending it.
